title: What is in the seventh book of the Cesti
english: Table of contents. These things are in the seventh book of Africanus's Cesti: 1. On arming. 2. On the destruction of enemies. 3. On athletic contest. 4. For the cutting of one who has been struck. 5. For a wound from iron. 6. Taming a horse. 7. That a horse may not neigh. 8. For a horse's cataract. 9. That a horse may not be startled. 10. On the speed of horses. 11. The horse-frightener. 12. For the destruction of pack-animals. 13. For a kicking mule. 14. Military hunting. 15. To find the breadth of a river and the height of a wall. 16. Theft of sound. 17. A means of staying awake. 18. For a fight against elephants. 19. Paradoxes of farming. 20. A seal concerning the missile.
translator_notes: Greek locked from PG 10 / Khazarzar Cesti fragmenta, book 7 pinax. Restorations in angle brackets are in the lock (book-number zeta; wall-height). One numeral before horse-taming is blank in the lock; the list is otherwise 1-20.
No public-domain English of the Cesti body exists; ANF has the letters only.

title: Outcomes come by reason, law, fate, or chance
english: Proem. The issues of affairs — births and destructions, alterations and healings — come by reason, or by law, or by fate, or by chance. It is good to know each of these, gathering from them all a varied profit that bears fruit: a therapy of sufferings, or a hidden history, or beauty of speech. These things, in what has gone before and in what follows, have been achieved, as I think, according to my own modest measure.
translator_notes: Greek locked from PG 10 / Khazarzar Cesti book 7 proem. Restoration ἰάματ<α> is in the lock.

title: Heavy Greek panoply, not numbers, turns the fight
english: On arming. It is a good thing, in all matters, to know war as well. I have often wondered at the cause of the differing turn of armed contests, and from this that Greeks have beaten Romans, and Persians have beaten Greeks, and yet the Persians have not yet been beaten by the Romans, but the nations of upper Asia dare to claim freedom and force an equal rank toward us.

Giving an account to myself, I found the cause was not superiority of stratagems, nor soldierly strength as a whole (for among good men numbers count for nothing in war), but the preparation of the weapons and the form of the war-dress.

The Greeks delight in a heavy panoply: a double felt cap, a scale breastplate, a hollow bronze-faced shield held by two grips — one about the forearm, enough for shoving, the other held by the end of the hand — two greaves, a javelin in the hands, a close-fighting spear equal to that of the royal horsemen, and a broad sword that is not long. With this arming a run is rare: not far, but sharp, and only so much as a man pressing on needs in order to get inside missile-range in time.

They also knew how to lock shields together, and each of them fought on his own, so that the soldier's virtue was double: in common and alone. They used to cut down the barbarians in this way: they rested themselves often on the march, so that eagerness would not be blunted by the length of the road, and so they stayed fresh in this manner up to the dangers. Then, using sharp speed to get inside the missiles, they had work to do, the missiles flying farther over them once they had run in under the fall, while the others, because the infantry fought lightly armed, could not endure the charge of such a fence. For the power of a missile is length; at close quarters the safety of the fight is accomplished by the panoply.

So, that they may suffer nothing from afar, the breastplate is stronger than every missile by the folding of the scales, that it may remain unwounded; and the felt about the head, having a cap, and another overlay of bronze, and one helmet upon another, answers the shots from a sling, the outer scale being crushed and yielding so that what is sent may not reach the inner covering of the head. The face is bare and the neck free, so that looking round in every direction goes unhindered.

With the spears some hold off the lance-bearing horsemen, striking first before they fall on; others, setting their phalanxes more openly and opening a way, reach the barbarians. They also use peltasts and slingers without danger, screened in front by the wall of the arms. The short swords are useful for ease and for the violence of the blow. The Macedonian successors altered few of these things, because of the variety of their wars, and fitted out an arming common both against barbarians and against one another.
translator_notes: Greek locked from PG 10 / Khazarzar Cesti 7.1 On arming. This slice ends at the Macedonian successors; the lock-file remainder continues in u01-rem.
Bracketed Greek ὅπη δεῖ ἐλλεβοροστρῶσαι in the lock is left unrendered as a suspected interpolation; no English was invented for it.

title: Alexander’s cap, the shaved beard, and the Roman kit
english: A sign that the fighters' faces were left free under a Laconian felt cap in the Macedonian arming: they call this thing, and this practice, the soldier-king's. Alexander himself ordered the soldiers to shave their beards, and when someone rebuked him for shearing off the ornament of the face, he said: "You do not know, you unmilitary man, that there is no more convenient grip in a fight than a beard." Coming to close quarters with this arming, no barbarian would hold out, however he was equipped.

The Romans have a helmet of a single material, leaving the faces a little open for breath and sight, reaching down to the shoulder-blades, and tightening the neck so that it cannot turn; a chain-mail breastplate; one greave; a long sword; and a rectangular shield carried as a screen by the end of the hand. In the locking of shields this is weaker for the body, because the soldier cannot throw his whole shoulder into the weapon. Their spears are shorter than the Greek.

They fight with success against the panoply already described. They have safety from things nearly equal, but they have the advantage in lightness: they are easy for attacks and withdrawals, quicker at taking high ground, and by the use of the long sword they are ready to strike the Greek neck, getting the blow in before the close fight. They too have trained every art of fighting at close quarters, so that the experience is equal on both sides, and the advantage is the lightness of the dress.
So that the point of their spears may not be blunted, and so that they may not be broken against the Greek breastplates, they fitted a missile with skill and, pushing, pierced the scales.

So those who have always been beaten by the Greeks — the very men who have almost always beaten the Greeks — rarely beat them. The first cause is this: they do not rush at a run into the clash, so as not to leave the baggage behind; they are always shut up in the brick-shape of the army; and they go down on the knee, tiling the army with overlays of shields, in their eagerness to spend the Parthian missiles. This practice makes them both idle and unharmed, worn by sun and toil, while the barbarians come on in relays and withdraw again, resting by the interval-sendings of the nations. Further, no Roman fights by himself, nor does any become a champion fighting the mass in single combat.
translator_notes: Greek locked from PG 10 / Khazarzar Cesti 7.1 remainder after the Macedonian successors. Restorations <τὸ>, <τοῦτο>, <δ'>, <μὴ> are in the lock.
οἱ τοὺς Ἕλληνας σχεδὸν εἰπεῖν ἀεὶ νενικηκότες is kept as the Romans, who have almost always beaten Greeks, rarely beating those the Greeks always beat.

title: What the Roman kit still lacks against barbarians
english: Shots from a sling that hit the heads crush the helmet and go in; and it is hard to duck a missile in flight because of the piece of iron about the neck. Besides this they do not throw the javelins with aim, spending ten on one possible kill, and they do not meet charging horsemen with small pikes.

If then someone put a Greek breastplate and helmet on a Roman soldier, and gave him a longer pike, and taught each man to throw each of the spears at each mark and to fight on his own, and sometimes set a run so that the charge inside missile-range against the enemy would be sharp, no barbarian, being cut down, would hold out against the Romans.
translator_notes: Closes Cesti 7.1 On arming. οὐκ ἂν βάρβαρος κοπτόμενος ἀρκέσειε Ῥωμαίοις: the barbarian would not suffice / hold out against Romans so equipped.

title: Do not make fortune mistress of the war
english: On the destruction of enemies. One must not fight the enemy in all things by close order and by battles, nor make fortune mistress of the whole of affairs. The end of war is unclear, and most things go contrary to expectation. Those better prepared in iron and men, or in bows and walls, have often been injured by wind, or sun, or place, or deceit, or a spectacle and an apparition; and in great wounds the daimon Pan is a constant.

The Phocians, better prepared in everything, did not receive the Thebans when they saw them crowned with laurel: the men who did not fear the war fled the crown. Wind and sun, meeting them in the face, more injured Flaminius and Paulus. The narrowness of the Gates made Leonidas equal to the five hundred myriads. Pan ran with the Athenians to Marathon against the Persians. Themistocles drove Xerxes from Greece by a lie.

Some smear missiles with drugs so that every wound becomes fatal; others set their strength in woods. Some, as they flee, destroy the pastures first; many poison the wells. Alexander took the Alans by farming hellebore. So one must not attempt those who stand against us from the open only, but must also general against the enemy by many hidden arts.

This old Carthaginian law has been thought out: they honored generals who planned the best things even if they did not succeed, and they punished those who attempted something rash and accomplished it, making the judgment not of fortune but of purpose. Fine too is the old iambic: the safe leader is more profitable to all than the rash.

The arts of generalship are very many, and there is nothing that happens that is not written down, to teach so that those things may not happen: healthy and well-watered camping-places, seizures of higher ground, ditching, advance-guards, night-marches, forward-rides, searches, ambushes, scouts, good arming, foraging, and with sleep a sufficient preparation; toward the enemy, distrust in all things.

As for exposing how they do harm, these things are clear, I think, and known to those who have kept company with histories: drinks of theriac as a defense against poisoned missiles, and the same cure for corrupted waters. Salt-drinkings we would decline for most, because of the disgust of taking them.
translator_notes: Opens Cesti 7.2. θέα μα καὶ φάσμα kept as spectacle and apparition (print split). Πάν is the god Pan, not a Bible name. No Scripture quotation in this slice.
πεντακοσίαις μυριάσιν: five hundred myriads (the Persian host at Thermopylae in this telling).

title: Starve them, and arm with air and water
english: If you cut the enemies' trees you will keep the other side from hiding. For not needing the others' pasture, the fodder brought along is enough, and whatever else has been thought out for a long campaign, toward having plenty of supplies and toward suffering nothing hard from the enemy — which is also the first deed of valor, because not to suffer is much better than to do harm. Pyrrhus, at any rate, though he had the advantage of the Romans, was consumed.

Time first, and wearing, and famine, and destruction, must especially be used against barbarians, whose gathering of the army is for a season and not a lasting force, but plunder from a raid. They bring foods measured in days and a stated number of missiles, and when those are spent their flight is obvious. Why then hurry to meet enemies whom, if I wait, I shall see driven by their own time-limit? Famine comes on them overdue, the few foods spent in vain. Come then, let us not even permit those starving men to flee. Let destruction without iron hold them, an end without battle. Let us beat them with air as ally and water as helper; with the elements let us arm against them. I general a secret array; I use a fight that does not show. Let every enemy fall when he has breathed, when he thirsts, or when he has eaten; I make all things dangerous to him. Let him starve if he stays, and take plague so that he may not flee. Let us do the work of a great prayer. Air as ally emptied Athens when it was filled with Lacedaemonians, and such a condition held the Carthaginians in Sicily. The victors dedicate such wars to their own gods. Let us too imitate those gods: automatic fortune comes about under our art.

Food, then, thus: let us make breads that will nourish the last day, from animals which are written down at the end, in pentagon 1, in which, along a line, are laid the signs of the Lydian mode being taken in besides — a defective zeta and an inverted tau. Shut both together into a vessel, sealing the lid with clay so that there may be no breathing-out for the beasts consumed inside by themselves; then grind their remains and put them into the water from which the cake is mixed. You will do the same if you smear the ovens with this juice; but for those who bake, this is a danger. [lacuna] Having prepared enough of such foods, furnish them to the enemies in whatever way you can.
translator_notes: Pentagon αʹ with Lydian-mode signs (defective zeta, inverted tau) is Africanus's cipher for the animals used in the bread; the names are not spelled in this lock. Print lacuna <.....> after κίνδυνος left unrestored.
This is a military-encyclopedia poison recipe in the lock; it is translated, not recommended.

title: Poisoned bread, poisoned wells, poisoned water
english: It would happen without suspicion if someone, being careless, worked the carrying toward an easy raid of the enemies and a wished-for snatching of the things brought to them, or if someone, feigning a serious flight, yielded to those coming on of the camp fortified with such foods. These do not bring a one-day death, nor do they kill the user at once. A plague-art overtakes this man and the one who did not eat; it is mixed into all and passes to the messmate. Into a house, a city, an army, a nation the plot migrates. Such a fate an Erinys procures for them. These are just dinners of penalties against barbarians, disease pouring upon all and an inexorable disaster overtaking the enemies.

If we fear we may use such a preparation in vain, either because they do not use it from suspicion, or because they have learned this from deserters, then, having feasted them, let us release either the criminals or the captives beside them; those who have kept company with them will take plague at once. I send them a plotting kindness. Let us likewise give them to drink such a loving-cup.

Three kinds of animals which lie in the second pentagon, toward the signs of the highest of the high — a turned-back gamma and an upright gamma: chop these so that all become ichor, and boiling them with very much water until all the fat of the boiled is consumed, pour into the enemies' watering-place. The bodies of those who have drunk will swell, themselves and the pack-animals; then a swelling with pain will stand upon them, and a man seeing himself become another from another, not recognizing the present form, slow both for flight and for an end, waiting the neighboring death, will pray for the speed of a warlike onset, that he may cease, both punished by the tension of inflammation and hated by himself because of the ugliness, the panoply that was inflated on the former body not holding the man now, so as to take from him even the pretense of standing in the arms.

Harm the waters also otherwise: fill the wells with dung and stones; and if the water is abundant, by fish-oil poured into them and by sea-purple, which for a long time make all water undrinkable. A greater standing of waters, or a lake, the myrtle-spurge thrown in will damage. Thus we shall first hinder the enemies by the drink. Let no one think the barbarians of the east unlearned in these things.
translator_notes: Second pentagon (turned-back gamma + upright gamma) again conceals animal names. [οἱ πολέμιοι] is a lock gloss on αὐτοῖς.
τιθύμαλλος μυρσινίτης: myrtle-spurge. θαλαττίᾳ πορφύρᾳ: murex / sea-purple.

title: Poisoned wine and poisoned air
english: They themselves often harm those who come against them. Poisoning of wine. Pharisees once prided themselves on having killed a phalanx of Romans by a pretense of flight. They were feasting, as it seemed, then withdrew when the others came on, leaving the meal ready. But the wine was a plot, poisoned with lime quenched in it. Wine is also poisoned with saltpeter-foam, box, hemlock, and like methods; for these, eaten, are enough to harm and to put enemies in a terrible state.

Since then we have taken foods and drinks as allies, come, let us also use air and wind against them. A man can guard himself from eating and drinking from enemies; how will he guard breath, how shut out air? Through these I come upon them.

Poisoning of air. The thrissos is a Thessalian snake, red in color, like a drakontis in length (and the same is also much in Asia; Syrians call it bathanerathan), which is written next in the third pentagon whose signs are of the parhypate of the high, a defective beta and an inverted gamma; and the lion is another snake, different, for it is both small and large, but the small is more takeable for this (and it too is much born in Syria). Let both be shut together into a vessel, safely very tight; and let the sharpest sun look at the vessel. When then they have been destroyed by one another and by the marsh-air and by time, let the vessel, set toward the wind accustomed to carry continuously toward those men, be opened, so that the exhalation from it may go to the opponents, the breeze ferrying into the breaths of those plotted against. Examples of the working: a horse running by will fall, and a neighboring man, and a bird not flying over comes down from the air murdered, caught by a wind faster than a fleeing wing.

If somewhere also against us, either by art of those from a plot, or also from one of the elements, destruction should happen, I have taken the treatment in advance for escape from the plague, having set it out in the skins before these. Themistocles, generaling, promised the victory against the Medes to himself by the sea-fight coming to be of men who would sail round by sleeplessness — this too being a great advantage over the enemies: to snatch their sleep.
translator_notes: Lock headings [Οἴνου φάρμαξις] and [Ἀέρος φάρμαξις] rendered as short labels. Φαρισαῖοι kept as the print; the military anecdote may not be the Jewish sect.
Syriac name βαθανηραθὰν and the two geographic asides are in lock brackets. Third pentagon conceals the snakes.

title: Steal their sleep at night
english: Old emperors of the Romans used the thing more nakedly and more actively, bringing on at night to the camp of the opponents both the lightest infantry and, with them, trumpeter-horsemen, through whom they accomplished one of two things: either, catching the advance-guards and watches more careless, they destroyed those in the way, or they threw in a panic. Some both shot and threw javelins, and those sent from a sling, whenever they missed, were carried against tent or horse or weapon: the noise accomplished more than wounding, always striking the neighbor with fear. The trumpeters, riding round, sounded the war-note, so as always to furnish to those stationed at that point the impression that the enemies would fall on at any moment.

Then after day they led the camp out, by every means contriving not to join battle, and setting out the coming night like the one past, their own men resting with all leisure of day, or by the sending of others, and the same men always being plotted against to stay sleepless. Who does not know how unmanageable the things from this are? Pain of the head, bad eating, slackness of body from desire to sleep even somehow, the same condition succeeding night and day. Having done this next, we shall take the opponents at the first shout, made womanish by sleeplessness.
translator_notes: Closes Cesti 7.2. πανικὸν is panic (the Pan-fright of the previous chapter), not a Bible term. τεθηλυμμένους: made womanish / unmanned by sleeplessness.

title: The cock-stone and the athlete’s meal
english: Athletic contest. All those skilled in these things praise the stones found in the bellies of noble cocks as co-workers of virtue and victory. Worn either in leather, or carried under the tongue, they keep soldiers and athletes and gladiators well set, lasting, and not thirsty. Others tell another form and color of them: some crystal-like and rough, some black — those who speak truly. They are found in the winner when he is cut up, as if not the virtue of the bird but the nature of the stone had become the cause of prevailing.

Since then, whether worn under the mouth or about the arm, the stone either falls out or is cut round by an antagonist, one must use an unsuspected wrapping of much power. Let the cock that has won, prepared as is the custom, be eaten whole by the contestant, so that the flesh is stripped, all of it, and the bones kept whole and unbroken; then after the table let it be purified by fire. The bird, no longer of day but a messenger of victory that will be, making the eater successor of its own unbeatenness, migrates into the man as by virtue.

The son of Neocles used the stone and the food when fighting the Persians; and from there he legislated the cock-fights in Athens when it had been raised, and the Athenians after the Median victory led a victory-feast of cocks.
translator_notes: Cesti 7.3. ὁ Νεοκλέους is Themistocles. κατατυθέντι τῷ νικήσαντι: the winning cock cut up, not a human victor.
No Scripture in this slice.

title: A light hand and a sharp edge for the cut
english: For the cutting of one who has been struck. Since many are cowardly toward the necessary treatments from iron, fearing the pain from the healing more than the coming harm from not being treated, come, let us somehow comfort the hesitation of the pain, making the sufferers more confident to endure the healing.

Let the healer have a light hand, so that he may run the cut easily, and let him bring a sharp edge; for bluntness is painful. The helper, being ready for all things, must also sprinkle with the brick which lies in pentagon 4, in which, according to the pyramid-shape, are laid signs of speech and of striking of the high enharmonic: an inverted alpha and a turned-back gamma having a line behind.
translator_notes: Opens Cesti 7.4. δειλοί is cowardly, not weak. ἐπιπασάτω is sprinkle, not press. πλίνθος is the coded drug in pentagon δʹ (inverted alpha + turned-back gamma with a trailing line). Musical labels are lock cipher, not a Bible text.
No Scripture quotation in this slice.

title: Smear the iron that wounded, and spit the Roman phrase
english: For a wound from iron. For the one struck by iron this too is a cure of pain: one ought to smear the iron that wounded, then strike it against the wound. Let us say "ta ta" three times, while also spitting a certain Roman phrase which is laid in the pentagon set out, the fifth, toward the chromatic signs: an inverted alpha having a line behind, and a turned-back gamma having two lines behind.
The pain will then cease. Let the sons of physicians treat the wound, the sufferer readily furnishing himself to their touching.
translator_notes: Cesti 7.5. «τὰ τὰ» thrice is the lock's spoken charm, not a Bible lemma. Ῥωμαῖαν ῥῆσιν is a Latin phrase coded in pentagon εʹ; the words themselves are not printed. ἐπάφησιν is touching/application, not 'report'.
No Scripture quotation.

title: Vice sits next to virtue in horses too
english: Taming a horse. Unmixed virtue is rare among men, and so also among horses. Next to the good things sits a grudging vice, so that the fine may not appear clean. One man is eloquent but not grave; another generals but is not temperate; someone is brave, but being a braggart he did not keep beauty unstained for himself; and another in another thing both has the advantage and misses. The fine and the bad in horses are like that: swift but lustful, hunters but hard-mouthed, walkers but violent. Some will not take riders; others shake them off. Some rub against walls or plants. Some are mischief-makers by nature, others have been made so by their owners. They bite and kick and stand off and rear, either hating or despising their masters. I can tell of many, each destroyed in a different disaster and form of evils under horses.

The arts of colt-tamers, as far as they can, either check or correct the vices: scant food for the violent, castration for the lovers, muzzles for the biters, wolf-bits for the hard-mouthed, blows for the disobedient. But what would a man do against the one that has stood off, and has chosen to obey in no way, toward nothing, either of commands or of lessons? Just as the wildest beasts, taken full-grown, are not tamed, but even if for a little they seem to have become handy they still do not forget the former savagery, so also this creature is hard to turn once vice has grown old in it.

Since then blow and threat and art and feeding are weak toward such things, let a vice of nature be corrected by an art of nature. Let a writing also tame him — a writing he will not fear, will not suspect, and wearing which he will be broken. In the hollow of the hoof of the front left foot, with the left hand, engrave with a bronze graver, on a sixteenth-day moon, a threat of a Roman command. The writing has a necessity of obedience. It lies in the pentagon whose numeral is blank in the lock, in which have been written the signs of the high diatonic: phi and digamma.
translator_notes: Cesti 7.6. λύκοις are wolf-toothed bits, not live wolves. σελήνης ἑκκαιδεκαταίας is the 16th day of the moon. Pentagon numeral is blank in the lock (as in the pinax before Ἵππου τιθασία); signs φῖ καὶ δίγαμμα.
No Scripture quotation.

title: Silence a horse by binding the tail
english: That a horse may not neigh. Horses neigh, some as a threat, others when they have taken only the smell from the females. Both their voice and their silence are useful. When they charge they are taught to shout together into fear with the fellow-soldiers; when they lie in ambush, to hide together with them. But this artificial thing is blunted still more either by the season of the year or by erotic nature.

Aristomenes the Messenian took Lacedaemonians who were lying in ambush when their horses neighed, himself leading a mare. And again he himself set his ambush without danger, his horses having been forced to be silent by a station of Spartan mares. The Messenian's stratagem remains remembered. So whether a man would go through a place infested with brigands, or would sit a cavalry ambush under the enemy, let him do what will be shown. This is not only a work and invention of old Greek generals: the Parthians also lead their own horses silent into the fights in this way.

With a well-twisted sinew the tail of the horse is bound tight above the hair, so that the bond sinks far into the surface. By the tension of the binding the horse, being in pain, keeps the same spirit and speed, but holds back only the voice, even if the compelling occasion is love.
translator_notes: Cesti 7.7. Aristomenes of Messene vs Spartan cavalry; the lock's θηλείας is a mare. Parthians kept as the eastern parallel. No Scripture.

title: Horses see daimons; ivy-juice for the cataract
english: For a horse's cataract. Homer wrote the Trojan horses as swift, but he made the Thessalian ones prophetic and gave them a human voice — not pointing out daimons, but exposing a horse-learning. Those now set over horses need to learn the divination from horses clearly, but they are unused to it. A horse's nod and look and voice and silence signify various things. I leave the rest aside: winters and prosperities and good years of fruits and their own offspring. The greatest: they both say and show the onsets of enemies; they also foretell murders; and they have often exposed hidden brigand-bands by a tension of the ears, or by hesitation of going forward, or by snorting.

And they have shown not only wicked men. Trust me when I say it: they see daimons too, and I know many that at crossroads neighed and fell and proclaimed the threat by the voice. Those of two unlike eyes seem to excel especially toward the understanding of such things, despising both war and apparition, and alone claiming against lions the kingship of the animals. Whether then it is a work of soul, or a nature of eyes, both must be trained: the one by teaching and art, the other by care.

Horses, like human athletes, must hold off from sex. This brings harm of the eyes; and much winter, having brought a chronic drip, does so too, and a cough besides. Let each affection be treated — the cataract — with the Bacchic plant. Treatment of horses that have the cataract: ivy juiced and mixed with the material already named; let it be an ointment two days running; then, the next being skipped again, let this be three times and often, until the horse recover the accustomed prophetic sight. I do not begrudge the treatment also to the second-rank beasts of horses. Use this for the cough; in a little you will find something lying inside.
translator_notes: Cesti 7.8. ἑτερόμματοι kept as horses of two unlike eyes (one-eyed / odd-eyed), not a moral metaphor. φυτῷ Βακχικῷ is ivy (κισσός) in the next sentence. μετ' ὀλίγον εὑρήσεις ἔνδον τι κείμενον points later in the Cesti, not a supplied recipe. Lock brackets on τὴν ὑπόχυσιν / μαντικήν kept as the print.
No Scripture. Homer is named; no Bible verse.

title: A living-beast’s tail on the right ear
english: That a horse may not be startled. For horses not being startled in vain by new sights or shadows, a cure is a tail attached to the right ear of the animal, cut from the beast while it was living. It lies in pentagon 7, over which are set the signs of hypate meson: sigma and sigma.
translator_notes: Cesti 7.9. Pentagon ζʹ (hypate meson, sigma+sigma) conceals which beast's tail. ὠτὶ δεξιῷ is the right ear. No Scripture.

title: Wolf-teeth on the bridle for speed
english: On the speed of horses. The speed of horses is blunted and it increases. [The lock marks the next clause corrupt:] a wolf as a counter-charm stands to each, and the two feet go numb; more quickly it comes to earth under a wolf. Wolf-feet are a possession horsemen seek after, and an astragalus of the same beast, hung on, also checks a runner. Rare, then, is the wounding and thinning that can happen.

We found another way the wolf can help toward swiftness, without harm to the horse. The canine teeth, taken out of a living wolf, are woven into the neck-pieces and contribute to both: they are an unsuspected help, and an ornament of contest-trappings. It is a fine thing if a man attach it to the whole four-horse team; if not, even the lead horse alone, having this wrapping, is enough to make the co-runners faster.
translator_notes: Cesti 7.10. Daggered clause λύκος ἀντιπαθὲς … ὑπὸ λύκου γίγνεται is translated word-for-word and left marked corrupt; no reconstruction invented. ἀστράγαλος is the ankle-bone. κυνόδοντες from a living wolf go into περιδεραίοις (neck-pieces / breast-trappings).
No Scripture.

title: The Sybarite horses that danced to the pipe
english: The horse-frightener. The story is that the Sybarites once drove luxury to this point: they would lead the horses into the symposium at dinner. The horses, having heard an aulos-tune, stand up on the two hind feet and dance with the front as if gesturing with the hands. An aulos-player who had been insulted deserted to the Crotoniates, freshly beaten in a horse-fight. He promised to benefit the common thing to the greatest degree, for he would hand over the whole Sybarite horse-force captive. The Crotoniates trusted him and allowed him to general. He gathered the city's aulos-players, showed the tune, and when it was time passed the word for the sally upon the enemies.

When the Sybarites came on with the whole people, snorting quite with the surplus of horse, and the phalanxes mixed with one another, under one signal all piped. The horses, having heard the accustomed sound as they had been taught at home, shook off the riders and all danced. Then the horsemen were caught lying, and the horses were taken dancing, the accustomed tunes having set them up.

Others also, being about to fight, pray — and they also sacrifice, having stood in contest — to Taraxippos Poseidon. We too found a drug quicker than prayer, better than all you might have, whose form has been inscribed at the end in pentagon 8, over which are set the signs of parhypate meson: rho and an inverted sigma. It is put into pus-extractors and in the array is given to light men to carry, so that they may stand easily under the press of the front-fighters.

Those then come on having trusted in strength and speed and iron. Whether they happen to be cataphracts, or equipped otherwise, they hurry into the same danger. For when the charge into the infantry has happened, the front-ranked bear the onset by the fence of the shields, and those holding the pus-extractors squeeze the drug into the horses' breaths (the juice is terrible even to men for harm). When the horses receive the smell of the evil they go mad and snort and stand up in haste, as if they had feared the breath from the earth, and they leap upright. The riders fall from the horses to the ground, ready for capture and for slaughter together, fettered by their own breastplates against escaping, either trampled or struck.
translator_notes: Opens Cesti 7.11. Taraxippos Poseidon is the horse-frightener hero/god; not a Bible name. πυουλκοί are surgical pus-extractors used as syringes for the coded drug in pentagon ηʹ. This is a military-encyclopedia recipe; translated, not recommended.
No Scripture.

title: Turtle-bile, and Dercyllidas’s pits
english: It is possible also to take a trial of this drug even at leisure, and to wonder how much strength there is from it, and in war better than missiles. A horse would fall otherwise, the nostrils sprinkled with the bile of a sea-turtle; and, given up by his own, it is our gain. For he will stand up if someone mix saffron and myrrh together with lily equally and apply it to his snout. Fallen mules will also stand up. But the juice of karpasos is more death-dealing to horses. They would also die if they became entangled with phalangia and with a salamander, and with ivy-tear and storax-juice. They are harmed too by the smoke from a menstrual rag. Let these things have been said otherwise.

Dercyllidas the Lacedaemonian, having brought an infantry phalanx against the opponents' horse, stationing them in the brick-shape and back-to-back in depth, ordered those behind, sitting under the shield, to dig pits with the daggers as fast as possible. Then he led the hoplites into the middle; and they were a defense. For the pits are most hostile to the horsemen.
translator_notes: Closes Cesti 7.11. καρπάσου kept as the lock's plant-name (not supplied as flax or aconite). ἀφέδρου ῥάκους is a menstrual rag. Dercyllidas's πλινθίον is the same brick-formation as in 7.1. No Scripture.

title: A drench against the killing disease of pack-animals
english: For the destruction of pack-animals. A horse that has fallen sick is a hindrance to a soldier, and so is a pack-animal carrying arms in war, and a pack-mule carrying the necessaries. To all these such a treatment of both the other affections and the plague-affections must be brought.

Treatment of sick cattle. Three half-xestai of celery seed; and four-thirds as much linseed; of fenugreek, double the second; of ground vetch, quadruple the fenugreek: these by measure. Of allheal-root and of Illyrian iris and of savin of the Sabine grass, forty-eight drachmas each; and quadruple the three together, the weight of old unsalted axle-grease. Each of the dry things named is chopped separately and sieved, and is dusted with old wine and the fat; then, shaped into little cakes, it is dried in the shade. At need, as much as a royal walnut's size (which weighs seven grammata) is pounded with three kyathoi of honey, then dissolved in the oldest and most serious wine; let it be one xestes. Taking it in for three days of each year, the beast will not suffer the killing affection of cattle. For the sick, instead of the wine, it is dissolved in water, of those who introduced the equal before.

If need should arise to use bran also, even from the sick constitution, in the absence of the cakes, drench three rolls soaking them in wine, the way many insert axle-grease by itself. Those for whom wolves are hunted most easily heal the pack-animals of the affections named thus: cutting broad thin steaks of wolf-flesh, they dry them lean, hanging them over smoke, such as we do of cattle. At need one must boil some of these until it melts, and mixing with the water a half-xestes each of wine and of oil, drench each year. A head cut off from a dog already dead and rotten also loosens that terrible affection for the sick horse; smoked by the continuous exhalation of the smell, he will be healed.

A more various and more many-ingredient composition. The most many-ingredient, of which I myself had trial, which the leading Romans use, it is necessary to learn: as much as eight drachmas of cluster-amomum and of each pepper, black and white — [lacuna] the double; triple of leaf and of pyrethrum and of aristolochia, and of wormwood and of hyssop and of the dirty iris; and still of gentian the quadruple.
translator_notes: Opens Cesti 7.12. Title πρὸς ὑποζυγίων φθοράν is a remedy against pack-animal destruction (veterinary), not a weapon against the animals. Lock lacuna after white pepper left unrestored. πίτυι rendered bran with the lock's dative kept in mind (pine is the other reading of πίτυς). Units kept: hemixestes, drachma, gramma, kyathos, xestes.
No Scripture.

title: The many-ingredient Roman drench, and a coughing horse
english: Fivefold — namely of the first — of spikenard and of aromatic calamus, and besides of meum, pyrethrum, aloe, myrtles, costus, cassia, ginger, saffron-paste, and still of saffron, of rock-parsley, and of Ethiopian cumin. Each of these is chopped finely and sieved with an aromatic sieve. Taking from this with three fingers, mix with one xestes of the finest wine, take in very little oil, then beat it moderately, and pour down the left nostril through the horn: to pack-mules and to adult pack-animals the complete mix; to horses half the mixture; and to three-year mules or two-year of the other beasts. To the healthy, each year, three times, which would be three days running. To the animal that has fallen sick of the killing disease it will likewise suffice, the rest of the care, as is reasonable, being brought to them from custom. Other things are needed against the smaller affections, and other things against the troublesome.

Treatment of coughing horses. For a coughing horse a treatment is hulled lentil, if you grind or pound it finely without the husks and give it to drink with water. The measure of the pulse for every animal by itself would be a fourth of a xestes, a fair amount. Every beast slack from toil, or fallen into upright-breathing, you would heal thus: give it lice or bedbugs pounded in wine, or the wet pitch together with barley-meal. You will not want for the other treatments, which lie scattered in these writings.
translator_notes: Closes Cesti 7.12. πενταπλάσιον (δηλαδὴ τοῦ πρώτου) continues the Roman many-ingredient drench from the previous slice. ὀρθοπνοίᾳ is breathing upright / respiratory distress. φακὸς ἐπτισμένος is hulled lentil. No Scripture.

title: Stop a kicking mule with box-seed
english: For a kicking mule. There is no use in a pack-animal that is healthy but mutinous, either otherwise disobedient or also kicking. For the obedience of horses the Roman voice is set forth. You will stop a kicking mule by boiling the seed of box and the caltrops in wine and giving it to drink; and for you she will remain tame for the months whose numeral is blank in the lock.
translator_notes: Cesti 7.13. ἡ Ῥωμαία φωνή points back to the hoof-inscription of 7.6. πύξου σπέρμα is box-seed; τρίβολοι are caltrops (the plant). Month-numeral blank in the lock; not supplied. No Scripture.

title: Hunt the lion with a tiled phalanx
english: Military hunting. Instead of exercise, hunting of lions will also be attached to an army. Lions catch the swift by speed, and pull down the strong by strength. No one of men would take them alive by force, but by timing and art and engine: what does not come by strength is accomplished by thought. The most hegemonic of the beasts — lightest and fastest and most fight-ready — is taken by various manners, of which, in this writing, I will recount those useful to an army.

When the war-leader will exercise together with the army and will approve a hunt, he leads all the infantry out to a hunt dressed in the war-gear. The trackers of the strong beasts have announced the mark where a lion dens. Quietly therefore, having come on, man holding to man, they stand in a circle, throwing the shields round and fitting them both toward one another and upon one another, so that their overlay is an image of roof-tiles. The trumpets sound vehement, and the men shout together loud. The beast leaps from the den disturbed, and having seen both the wall of the hoplites and burning torches being brought (for the hoplites carry these instead of spears), he is quiet and remains and does not leap over the press of the shields.

Where the ground is more downhill, a machine is brought on which a broad and spread-out cage is set, carrying a kid. Behind the lion, men in full armor, having dry and whole hides, shout in, striking with woods. Struck by the sound and the sight and the cry, he rushes at a run upon the cage — the hoplites behind the machine having leaned down and being unseen by the beast, and those around the cage walled with high boards — so that, seeming to escape by that way alone, he may be mastered. This then is one manner of hunting for a phalanx being exercised; the others I have recounted elsewhere.
translator_notes: Cesti 7.14. Restoration <λεόντων> / <τὰ στρατεύματι> are in the lock. κεράμων εἰκόνα is roof-tiles (the testudo overlay), not pottery as ware. γαλεάγρα is a cage. Africanus says the other manners are elsewhere; they are not supplied here.
No Scripture.

title: A Euclid cut to measure a river you cannot cross
english: To find the breadth of a river and the height of a wall. Those moderately possessed of encyclical education have, as is likely, touched Euclid's Elements to some extent. It is not hard, then, through the first book, to establish these things too: to measure the breadth of a river, the other bank being untrodden because of the enemies stationed on it, so as to bring on a matching span to bridge it; and by the same ratio to take the height of a wall from a distance, so as to bring up helepolis engines of equal standing.

For ease of learning the proof, this theorem will lead: “If one of the sides about the right angle of a right-angled triangle is bisected, and from the cut a straight line is raised at right angles, and through the point where it cuts the remaining side a parallel is drawn, the remaining sides of the triangle are also bisected.”

Let ABΓ be a right-angled triangle, having the right angle at B. Let AB be bisected at Δ. Let ΔΕ be drawn at right angles. Through E let EZ be drawn parallel. I say that the remaining sides of the triangle are also bisected: AΓ at E, BΓ at Z. Join ΔZ. Since AΔ is equal to ΔB, and ΔB to EZ, AΔ is therefore equal to EZ and parallel. And the lines joining equals and parallels on the same parts are equal and parallel. ΔΕ and ZΓ also make parallelogram ΓΕΔZ. ΔZ is therefore equal to ΕΓ. But it was also equal to AE. ΕΓ is therefore equal to AE. Again, since each of BΔ EZ and ΓΕ ΔZ is a parallelogram, ΔΕ is therefore equal to each of BZ and ZΓ, for they are opposite. So BZ and ZΓ are also equal. The proofs hold also for every triangle.

Following these things, the breadth of a river will be measured from a distance. Let there be banks: opposite, the enemies' bank, on which is point A; toward us, ΦΗ. A split dioptra is planted in a place toward us, at I, so that the interval from I to our bank of the river is greater than the river. This is easy to guess. Two points are sighted at right angles: one on the opposite bank — a stone or a bush or some other easy mark — and let it be A; the other, the point toward us, from the other line of the cross, Υ. Moving the dioptra onto Υ I sight A and make a right-angled triangle. Let IΥ be bisected at K.
translator_notes: Opens Cesti 7.15. Euclid Elements I construction; letter-points kept. διόπτρα is the sighting-instrument; ἑλέπολις the siege-tower. Restoration <ὕψος> is in the lock. No Scripture.

title: The same ratio for the river, then for the wall
english: From K let KΘ be drawn parallel to AI, and from Θ let ΘΡ be drawn parallel to IΥ. Since then of right-angled triangle AIΥ, IΥ has been bisected at K, and ΘΚ is parallel to AI and ΘΡ to IΥ, AI too is bisected at Ρ. Measure off the interval from I to Ρ. The interval from Ρ to A is therefore also given. Subtracting from this the interval from Ρ to Φ, we shall have the rest: that is, the breadth of the river.

If it seems laborious to someone to take a larger interval standing off on our own land, the sight there being of necessity disturbed and the result confused, we may, standing on the same bank of the river, easily take the magnitude of the breadth in this way. Again let point A have been taken on the opposite part. On the part toward us let point B have been taken, so that AB is at right angles to the line through the bank, BΓ. Some point Δ has been taken on BΓ, on which let rod ΔΕ lie. At the end of the rod let gnomon E be raised, so that if rod ΔΕ should touch the surface of the water, the gnomon is at the surface. Let the rod be carried, at right angles to ΔΕ, along BΓ, until from some point Γ on line BΓ, through a dioptra, points E and A are seen. It will be analogon: as BΓ is to ΓΔ, so AB is to EΔ. The ratio of BΓ to ΓΔ has been given. The ratio of AB to ΔΕ has therefore also been given. And ΔΕ is given. AB is therefore also given.

By the same ratio the height of a wall will also be taken, on the same diagram set upright. Let the top of the battlement be A, the base B, and the line from the wall to us, outside missile-range, BΓ. A dioptra hangs from a pole (which is called a “lampstand”), planted at right angles at Γ. Let the pole be line ΔΓ. Tilting the dioptra, I sight the top of the wall, which is A. Going to the other vessel, on the same straight I take point E. Triangle AEB it will be, and parallel to one of the sides, AB, is ΓΔ. The ratio that ΕΓ has to ΓΔ, this EB has to BA. The ratio of ΕΓ to ΓΔ has been given, for each of them has been given. The ratio of EB to AB has therefore also been given. EB has also been given, as was shown on the river. BA is therefore also given, which was to be shown.
translator_notes: Closes Cesti 7.15. Second method stands on the same bank with rod and gnomon. Wall height uses a pole called λυχνία (lampstand) and a hanging dioptra. Restorations in the lock kept. No Scripture.

title: Mauretanians hunt hearing; a well steals camp talk
english: Theft of sound. The Mauretanians see sharpest of all. They recognize one approaching from far off, and they hear equally, though hearing is slower than seeing. Their sight is long by exercise and by nature: besides the runs they train, breathing very light air, they also abstain from everything hot and from salts, as being causes of dim sight.

So that they may never be caught sleeping, and an approach of enemies not escape them at night, they set under the neck that sleeping-wood of theirs, leaving the ear unhindered for hearing, dig a little pit, and hear both from far off — both voice and shouts. I have heard that the brigands of the western Gauls do the same. This is an improvised hunting of hearing.

If someone in a great camp should wish to learn the counsels of his own soldiers, or the secrets of the enemy — Art of knowing things to come — having dug a deep well, let him let down whom he wants, covering the mouth with some cloak. Nothing will escape the one sitting in it; he will recount to you what was said or what sounded, as if prophesying.

Let everyone trust my word: the one hunting long hearing by sitting with it, and the other, on a lightless night, to see something hidden on the earth, reasonably without fire. For the higher air is full of sound, and the plain earth strikes the sight with thickness and dulls the hearing with noise.
translator_notes: Cesti 7.16. Μαυρούσιοι kept as Mauretanians. Lock heading [Τέχνη προγνωστικὴ τῶν μελλόντων] rendered as a short label. εὐναστήριον ξύλον is the sleeping-wood under the neck. No Scripture.

title: Sleep outgenerals Zeus; a membrane-winged head keeps watch
english: A means of staying awake. The poets put Zeus to sleep, outgeneraled by Hera and Sleep, so that either the Greeks might catch their breath, or Heracles be harmed; they also often make rivers stand still.

We ourselves have observed how the current is quiet at night, so that one might say the water is found sleeping. The breaths of the winds too are gentler than the night; perhaps these also are calmed by sleep. It is superfluous to say that heroes have been caught by Sleep's swoop.

He rules all: men, birds, plants, waves, winds, gods; all-subduer and limb-loosener, occupying souls away from bodies. Death is his brother, and Toil a fellow-worker; they toast one another the evil misfortunes of those about to sleep.

The commander of Ilium expected to take the Achaean “worn with toil and with sleep,” but the care on that side stood equal against him. How much would the Thracians have valued the wakefulness of Rhesus, a noble king betrayed by toil and sleep? No one was struck with awe at his fine panoply; no one feared his swift horses. How many hopes of success has the sleep of a single hour overturned?

From this the stratagem has come down to later times: they leave much wine in the camp for enemies following under the appearance of flight, so that even if a man has not toiled he may sleep at least from drinking; and others, coming on here and there at night, kill them as they rise, still sleeping. Panics too often arise in camps for one frightened in sleep.

We pity human fortune; let us remedy the outrages of untimely sleeps by a daimonic passion. The Phrygian king found Silenus sleeping and bound him; another fortunate commander bound a satyr. I do not think myself unworthy of equal honor with them. They took earth-dwelling daimons, humble ones, asleep; I seek to take the one who bound them. I want Sleep to become inferior to my experience, so that this king and all-subduer may dwell with me alone.
Let a king in council stay awake with me, and a soldier on guard, and a champion who has toiled. I array myself against you, Sleep: as you campaign against all, so I will campaign against you.

There is a winged animal, membrane-winged, living in dark places, of which alone among the egg-laying winged creatures the young are fed with milk. Its skeletonized head, sewn into a little piece of leather, makes the one who hangs it about himself sleepless as long as he wears it.
translator_notes: Opens Cesti 7.17. Poets: Hera and Sleep vs Zeus (Greeks breathe / Heracles harmed). ἱστᾶσιν ποταμούς: Sleep stills rivers, not 'they set up rivers'. Quote καμάτῳ ἀδηκότα ἠδὲ καὶ ὕπνῳ ~ Il. 10.98; Rhesus Il. 10. Restorations ἀνέ<μων>, <οὗ μόνου> are in the lock. Membrane-winged milk-fed animal is the riddle creature; name held for pentagon θʹ. Homeric, not Scripture.

title: Drink from the live wing, sew the head to the pillow
english: Let someone pull out a whole wing of it while it is alive and use it as a scraper-scoop for drawing drink — infrequently if for a short time, but often and with both wings if someone needs long watches. If someone uses this drink without measure, he will remain sleepless altogether.

If you should also wish to play a trick by throwing someone into sleeplessness, take the head of a living one and sew it to the pillow where it is his custom to sleep. He will not sleep, as if he had hung the whole creature about him; for it keeps sleepless throughout the one who wears it so.
You are Night's child, O Sleep; a bird of night beats you. Even if you happen to be winged, I too forestall you with another wing. Thus the marriage of Pasithea to Sleep.
Eros stays awake; and the theft of the wing is the pledge under Hera of this. What wonder if Hera received this too from the Charites? For she borrowed the cestus-bands from Aphrodite.

If then you recognized the animal from the tokens — for it is not set out unclearly or hard to grasp — you might perhaps be praised. If not, you will find it lying at the end in pentagon 9, toward the signs of the middles of the enharmonic Lydian mode — and it is toward the last ones — pi and a reversed sigma.
translator_notes: Closes Cesti 7.17. λιστρίον is a scraper used as a scoop from the live wing, not a stirrer. Pasithea and the borrowed cestus are Iliad 14, not Scripture. Lock prints Ἥρατούτου (crux; English takes Ἥρας τούτου). Χαρί των is Χαρίτων. Lock ἀγρυπνοῦσι with singular Ἔρως kept as number-mismatch; English 'Eros stays awake'. Pentagon θʹ, Lydian enharmonic meson, π + reversed ς. Animal name not supplied in the reading text.

title: An elephant is a walking wall; do not set horse against it
english: For a fight against elephants. The ancients thought elephants a great help in the fights: to strike with fear horses unaccustomed at the first spectacle, and men; and themselves, having been towered, to be a fear, as if a wall were walking before the phalanx. The clang is sharp, and the charge unbearable. The tusks are sufficient even otherwise for the overturn of every crowd; they also fitted to them spear-points analogous to the size, fenced most of them with broad breastplates, and even gave the beasts javelins to throw with the trunk. It was a portable phalanx, an image of every kind of war having the advantage: from above, the sendings of missiles of many men on high; at the feet, things unfightable; and hostile flights even far off. The fight is not from equal honor; one had to fight a wall against the elephant.

The crowds, overturned, the shield-lock always having been broken, furnished easy to the opponents the loosened order for destruction, as if, a bronze-mouth trireme having been broken by a very small charge, the whole surge, roughened, dissolved. Who will withstand the bearing of a crag that has broken? A fighting elephant is the image of a mountain. He overturns, throws down, breaks, destroys; and he does not disdain even the man lying, in the manner of noble beasts. Drawing with the trunk both horse and man and chariot, bringing them down by force and turning them, he drags them as far as his own feet; and leaning on the knees, he crushes them even otherwise, having perceived his own burden, and then is heavier still by the putting-on of the towers, so that a man is not pressed by one elephant, but is destroyed by a meeting of much heaviness.

How should one ward off a beast hard to fight, armed both with many advantages from nature and with the arts of men? He overturns the standing, overtakes the fleeing, crushes the fallen, frightens the horseman, strikes the chariot-drivers from the tower. First, then, one must set light javelin-men and bowmen against them, and no longer station cavalry against them, so that the army not be thrown together by the horses' fear from the unaccustomed sight. Let the trumpeters shout in terribly, so that the clang of the instrument, opposing the hiss of the beast, blunts the threat. Let the peltasts aim at the elephant, not using an unmissable mark; let the bowmen throw fire-bearing arrows onto the towers. For a chance missile stuck in is enough for the destruction of the whole.
translator_notes: Opens Cesti 7.18. κέρατα here are tusks. προνομαία is the trunk. Restoration <καὶ> / <φόβῳ> in the lock. Bracketed εἴκων and [τὸν] left as print. No Scripture.

title: Fire the tower; caltrops take the beast by its own weight
english: For the beast, having perceived the flame and feared the danger of the fire, shakes off the battlements laid on it — and one might liken it to a tower falling on a sacked city. If it is itself wounded in the bare parts, it has already feared the enemies, and having turned onto the friends it rages harder. Like a mountain flame or a torrent downhill, being angered it thus most of all kills, wounds, takes away, throws down, treads; and it hates the corpses themselves, heaps fallen bodies, and fences the roads of those fleeing, as if warding off the friends because it has suffered these things through them.

I, however, think it better not to stand against the elephant at the start, nor to go close to the multiplied danger, but to take in advance its threats, its charges, its fights, its fallings; for, encircled and fallen, it will destroy many. Iron caltrops are forged, sharp, seated, thick. These, along the going of the beasts, are thrown dense by those pretending to withdraw, and having been trodden they stop the elephant, having sunk into the hides of the feet. For by that with which it treads the others by weight, by this it is itself caught, treading itself whole. A double advantage from this: either, being in pain, it destroys its own, consoling an incurable pain; or, not being able to stand, it falls all together.

All spoils from wars are solemn; more solemn than all, an elephant bears. A general's shield is not so honorable, nor the breastplate of a champion who has been killed, as a living elephant captive, or the first-fruits of the elephant, to a king who has conquered.
translator_notes: Closes Cesti 7.18. τρίβολοι are iron caltrops. Bracketed ἱστᾶσιν ἔνδον left unrestored as a lock doublet. Restorations <ἢ>, <δὲ> in the lock. No Scripture.

title: Wine where the land will not give it
english: Paradoxes of farming. Nor indeed will agricultural matters be left out here, equally as everywhere; for they will have some things useful even to those at war. It is blessed, on the one hand, to farm all-bearing land in peace, receiving varied fruit of different seasons, to pluck, to reap, to vintage, taking abundant wealth from one country, not needing foreign goods, nor waiting on hopes from across the sea. But as things are now, not all countries bear all things: some, by excess of cold, nourish only grain-fields; sandy others vintage the vine or the olive; the much-spread plains possess and bear wine rarely, and some only a poor wine at that. Let us therefore furnish a device for both: to find wine when it is not, and the change of the poor into the better.

Let the measure of wine with water be tenfold; then let it be boiled with much fire, until the tenth of the mixture is consumed. There is a loss of the water, but a gain of the wine, which has become better in the virtue of which the flame is mother. Doing this the ancients reported that the fire midwifed Dionysus. Those who do not have vines, nor have been fortunate in the fruit from these plants, have imitated wine by a preparation of other seeds or tree-fruits, or by a composition of roots, declining the drink of pure water. The Egyptians, at any rate, drink zython, the Paeonians kamon, the Celts kerbesia, the Babylonians sikera. For Dionysus left them in anger and gifted them nothing of vine-culture, keeping the victory-prizes for Greek farmers alone. Let us imitate Dionysus; let us toast to men the friendship-cup without the cluster. I know other fruits that are makers of wine.

This, then, is a preparation of wine: one mina of dried figs, three choes of clean seawater, two bundles of licorice. Chop the roots and throw them into a jar from the fig, then again having passed a portion of the root through up to three times, and then pour on the sea — and under the vessel let there be horse-fennel, about two bundles — and let it soak five days and pour it off through a strainer, and let it be sweet. Then give sweet water the same measure and let it soak five days, and having strained this mix it with the former; then having stoppered it put it away in the shade, and it will be good wine. If, having poured water, you should let it soak upon these seven days, and having strained it you should throw in the pressed-husks from the jars and stopper it until the tenth day, you will make vinegar — but do it in winter.
translator_notes: Opens Cesti 7.19. Lock διαψιλῆ treated as δαψιλῆ (abundant). Restoration <αἱ χῶραι οὐ φέρουσι πᾶσαι> used. Bracketed ἀλαζὼν ὁ λόγος left as print, not in the reading text. ζῦθος / κάμος / κερβησία / σίκερα kept as drink-names. ἱππομάραθρον = horse-fennel. No Scripture.

title: Vinegar without spending the wine; Iberian oil
english: And the vinegar itself is not to be neglected. Vinegar is multiplied if, having boiled beet, you throw into the chous of water four drachmas of Cretan licorice and, having boiled it, you add one drachma of Greek nitre; with this preparation is mixed, to one measure of vinegar, double the water. Every vinegar is intensified when five drachmas of pepper, and of juniper equally, are mixed into the metretes.

The hope that concerns only the spoilage of wine is slow and is not a farmer's prayer; and I know vinegar forced into speed by all kinds of practices, the wine already having turned and changed for the worse. Some throw in burnt barley, some a potsherd that has been fired, and others iron. Honey is often thrown in too. I, however, will make vinegar self-grown and sweet, bringing use and pleasure, without the loss of the wine. For the squeezed grape-stone is enough: together with the marc it is soaked into water, so that the water takes the quality of must; then, thrown into a cauldron, it is fired underneath and boiled to the half, and having cooled it is transferred into another vessel. It changes, then, as mixed with water, but remains sweet as must boiled down.

Vinegar could also come without a grape. Pitch last year's full pine-cones with wet pitch and burn them round until the pitch is burnt off; then honey them all with a feather. Let there be water in a large vessel, and the cones about ten to each chous of water; throwing these into the wet, boil as much as to warm; let the vessel be short by cotylae — the numeral is blank in the lock. Having muzzled it all round, you will leave it in the sun three days; then having uncovered it, take off as much of the vinegar as you want and throw on the equal of water. Thus for a long time you will have vinegar unfailing.

One must be eager about the oil too. The Iberian somehow thus: a handful of wild-olive leaves, four drachmas of dry fenugreek, one of wormwood, and two drachmas of roasted lees which the Romans call "fecula." Chop all and make a handful-mass, then bind it in a rag, let it down into the jar, and after nine days draw it off for use. And you would have Istrian too: chop green leaves of bitter almonds, make a mass, throw it into the vessel, stir it, and let it settle. Mastic-oil is prepared thus: the ripe fruit of the mastic, thrown into a mortar, is chopped with a wooden pestle.
translator_notes: Continues 7.19. τεῦτλον = beet; γίγαρτον = grape-stone; στρόβιλοι = pine-cones. Lock κοτύλων with blank numeral unrestored. Roman φέκλα kept as fecula. σχῖνος = mastic. No Scripture.

title: Terebinth oil, foul oil made bright, and Lydian garum
english: Then it is poured down into vessels; soaked the longest time in boiling water and taken up, it is squeezed out with wicker baskets. Some, having chopped and mixed with water, set them in ovens until it is boiled, and thus squeeze them out. The terebinth-oil is prepared likewise to the mastic. Others, having chopped, throw them into pots that have a little water standing above, then boil and pick off the oily that floats on top (good oil comes off to the bottom of the jar, green dill and salt having been let down).

Black and dirty oil you will brighten thus: roast one litra of nitre, chop it, sift it, throw it into the jar. If you also want to make it like omphacinum, chop bark of wild olive and leaves, make a mass, and by weight throw a litra into a jar. If you want to make the Iberian I first said, which we name "Spanum," throw chopped wild-olive leaves into very clear Sidetic oil, having bound them in a proportionate linen and hung them, and let them soak as many days as you want; and thus it will acquire the Iberian quality.

You would heal turbid oil by pouring it into a wide-mouth vessel and setting it in steady sun, and sprinkling roasted salts sufficiently, toward the rewarming; whenever it has settled, transfer it into vessels. The foul-smelling thus: chop green olive without the pits, as much as a half-choenix, throw it into the metretes; set it in the sun and heat it enough, then take out what was thrown in and transfer into more vessels.

And from calf suet oil could come, even odorless oil: choes of pickled-olive brine — the measure is lost in the lock — throw into a bronze kettle, and of the suet in a basket ten minas; let it have a weight toward not floating, a stone laid in, and fire underneath with a soft fire. Taking off what boils up, throw it at once into a newly-emptied oil-jar; and of the suet having melted, filter the remainder with a strainer and throw it onto the vessel, and having taken it aside let it for twenty days; then use it. But also garum from one part of unmixed brine and two of the sweet wine. The serious one comes from Lydia; and the one named "soccius," which they praise more than all garums.
translator_notes: Continues 7.19 through garum. τερμίνθινον = terebinth-oil; ὀμφάκινον = oil of unripe olives; Σιδητικόν = Sidetic. Lock lacuna after κολυμβάδων ζωμοῦ χοᾶς. Bracketed σπυρίδι left as print beside θαλλίδι. σόκκιος kept as the named garum. No Scripture.

title: Abdomia, Libyan phriton, and the Roman apple
english: Of the so-called abdomia, ten xestai, and as much Libyan stagmas of fortunate Libya (which the locals call phriton), and a bundle of Cretan hyssop, and the Roman apple (called orbiclatum), mixing them with sixteen cotylai of honey, boil with a fig branch for three days and three hours each day on a gentle fire, and that too will turn out.
translator_notes: Closes the farming recipes of Cesti 7.19. ἀβδωμίων, φρίτον, ὀρβικλάτον kept as lock names. Restoration <σὺν> in the lock. No Scripture.

title: One arrow through a night and a day
english: A seal concerning the missile. Let this writing too end in some ancient and learning-loving tale, following those who have led: the tale of a bow and a missile. One missile, carried through a whole night and day, can come down as far as twenty-five thousand stades, if the motion were continuous.

About the flight of the missile it would be like this. Let some commensurate men, not more than ten, stand toward a mark of a measured plethron. Let them have bows ready, and let a missile lie on the string, so that the first hits the mark and a second throws straightway after him, and a third in sequence, and the others likewise, the second always resting his throw only so long as the first man's missile takes to reach the mark. I have seen some trying it, and I have the history from trial.

The number of the stades has been gathered somehow thus. Six plethra make a stadion. One missile was carried for each plethron. The missiles being numbered into one hour, not more than six thousand were sent in the hour. (Think and reckon the number of the missiles as the travel of one missile: give the examination to the interval, not to the multitude of those sent.) Therefore one missile — for let the many be measured as one by the rush of the interval — went through six thousand plethra from the beginning of the hour to its ending, which make a thousand stades. The intervals of the night and the day, cycled into twenty-four hours, set as twenty-four thousand. Let a thousand be added upon these, given to the leisure of each preparation, so that even the beginning of the delay not be without number. Still there is always inequality in the hours of day and night, and much of it. If then someone, having watched an equinoctial hour, should make the trial of the throw according to it, it will happen for him that they become twenty-five thousand stades.
translator_notes: Opens Cesti 7.20 (pinax κʹ Ἐπισφράγισμα περὶ βέλους). Restorations <τὸ>, <καὶ πεντακισχιλίων> in the lock. πλέθρον kept. Homeric/technical, not Scripture.

title: Mannos, Bardesanes, and Syrmos: the trial at Abgar’s
english: Syrmos the Scythian used this trial, and Bardesanes the Parthian, and perhaps even more somewhere. I saw it myself, in the house of Abgar the king, Mannos his son having often tried it, I directing. He was so terrible an archer that once, a hunt being around midday — I happened to be riding by, not as some hunter but as a spectator of the hunt — a woodland bear leaps out from some thicket, fearful to approach, terrible to see, perhaps even impossible to hit. All were startled and seeking the roads of flight. Mannos, exhorting us to take courage, dissolved all the fear by throwing two missiles: having shot the eyes of the bear, he made her easy to handle, not even seeing the hunters.

Bardesanes was a wise archer if anyone else was. I know a man who shot as a painter does. The manner was this. He once stood a man opposite, a youth beautiful and stout, whom even a painter would have tired imitating. The youth was holding forth the shield: Bardesanes ordered this, showing the art to us spectators. He, like a good painter, transferred the man holding it onto the shield. First he was drawing the head with upright missiles, imitating a circle of a head; then the casts of the eyes, the fittings of the lips, the rhythm of the chin; and the rest of the man followed the order of the body. He was priding himself, having taken painting together with archery: drawing with missiles and shooting drawings. We wondered, seeing that the shooting was not a warlike practice, but was something delightful too, and danger a pleasure. The youth, having laid down the shield, saw himself drawn upon his own weapon and was rejoicing, having become a soldierly painting. This, then, I have, having wondered.

What would I say of Syrmos? Syrmos too was a wise archer, not having painted with missiles as Bardesanes, but having devised to make a missile a hostile missile. New is the spectacle, but not unbelievable. I saw a missile under a missile. I saw a missile, and a missile being made ready, I was ready to throw. Someone else, a counter-archer, had stood against him from afar. Different was the contest of the archery: the one was contending with an armed missile, the other with a naked one. The mark for each was to join missile with missile. The one was meeting only, like a naked soldier against an armed enemy, and it was bold; the other, inasmuch as it had not been stripped, stuck into the one that met it and was drawing it, hung, as a hostile captive. The stripped one, having been taken, was no longer a missile, but the spoil of a missile.
Cestus 7 of Julius Africanus.
translator_notes: Closes Cesti 7.20 and the book: Ἰουλίου Ἀφρικανοῦ Κεστὸς ζʹ. Abgar and Mannos at Edessa; Bardesanes the Parthian. Lock repeats Καινὸν τὸ θέαμα once; both kept. Restorations <καὶ ζητούντων>, <ἦν>, <τὸ δὲ> in the lock. The lock then prints an appendix (dyeing wood as ebony) and a pinax that belongs with book 2; those are not in this section. No Scripture.

title: Wine that puts drinkers to sleep for three days
english: How through wine one might work upon those who have drunk, so they sleep for three days. Enviable is the man who is not without such a drug: for if he will have the means to prepare wine from this, those who have used this drink sleep, so that those who have drunk are even caught by the enemy sleeping up to three days. They will rise if someone should anoint their nostrils with vinegar.

The preparation of this is as follows. Two parts of Theban opium, as in a dose: pound these smooth with one part of henbane juice, and pound the dirt from the right ear of a donkey, and throw it into the wine.
translator_notes: Opens Cesti book 2 (book-2 pinax held). ζηλωτός is the adjective enviable, not Zealots. ὄξος is vinegar, the waking antidote on the nostrils. Theban opium + henbane juice + dirt from a donkey's right ear. ὡς ἐν θέματι kept as a dose. No Scripture.

title: Destroy enemy fields with hellebore and salt
english: On the destruction of fields. There are times, travelling through hostile land, when you will attempt to destroy its fields, farming hellebore; for Alexander the Macedonian, using this manner, took the Alans. Fields are also destroyed by salts being sown in them and covered with ploughs; for a long time this can put them in a very bad state.
translator_notes: Cesti 2.2. Same hellebore stratagem as book 7 vs the Alans. Restoration τοῦ<το αὐ>τούς in the lock. No Scripture.

title: Dry fruit trees, except the apple
english: On the destruction of trees. It seems right to us also to destroy the fruit-bearing trees of the fields, so that the enemies, often lacking foods, may not find the fruits instead of food. You will dry every tree except the apple, if you plant the sting of the sea stingray into the stem of the tree. The Quintilii say that the husks of beans, put to the roots, dry these. I rather am pleased, speaking of all that have grown for beauty, that these be cut down; for when this has been done, no enemy hides in the cut, no bird sits over them for hunting — which is complete destruction.
translator_notes: Cesti 2.3. θαλαττίας τρυγόνος is the stingray. μηλέας excepted. Κυϊντίλιοι = the Quintilii. Restoration <ἀποροῦντας>, φι<λο>κάλως in the lock. No Scripture.

title: A wolf’s right-fore ankle-bone stops horses
english: On making horses unmovable from the same place. Laboring at the exposition of the present writing, I read in Neptunianus's Physica that a wolf's ankle-bone of the right forefoot, thrown before a four-horse team, stops the chariot. If then it stops four, how much more when in battle-line we give one each to a few slingers? When they have thrown these into the enemy's horse, not only will the one ankle-bone harm one horse, but as many as happen to ride past through it.
translator_notes: Cesti 2.4. Νεπτουνιανοῦ Φυσικά. λύκου ἀστράγαλος of the right forefoot. Restoration <ἂν> in the lock. No Scripture.

title: Scythian arrow-salve from palisade spurge
english: Anointing of arrows. Scythians anoint arrows with the so-called toxicon for the swift killing of those they wound. When I was seeking this, a trustworthy man gave me the drug set out below, which produces the same effect.

It is this: take the palisade-spurge, which rises into stalk-like branches; put it into a newly made earthen vessel and boil it with water until it releases all its fat into the hot water. Then draw up the woods of the plant that were put in, and throw other green ones into the same water. Draw them up again and, throwing in others, boil until the water from their juice becomes honey-like. I do not have confidence whether this has been made safely. Some of the ancients say that the venom of the viper, and of the asp and the salamander as well, is unfailing for this.
translator_notes: Cesti 2.5. τιθύμαλλος χαρακίτης is the palisade/characias spurge, not wool. τοξικόν is arrow-poison. ἄγγος νεουργὲς ὀστράκινον is a newly made earthen vessel. πιμελή is the plant's fat/grease; ὀπός the sap. Africanus will not vouch the recipe is safely made. Ancients add viper, asp, and salamander venom as unfailing (ἀσπίς here the asp, not a shield). No Scripture.

title: Keep soldiers well: little meals, rue, wormwood, squill
english: On the health of the soldiers. That a physician is a good thing in an army is unambiguous. So that a soldier not be sick, struck by sun and toil, one must divide their foods for this: not once or twice, but little and often in the day, and especially when a contest is not present. For this is saving and suitable toward digestion.

It is necessary, having boiled rue and wild mallow and mixed them with turned wine, to take them in the middle of the foods; likewise, having mixed milk and water and poured on a little turned wine, to take it before eating. This must be done from the beginning of spring until the end of autumn. And again wormwood-wine is drunk to the same end, not only before food but also after food and in the food itself. If we have no wormwood-wine, let us give wormwood with hot water. Squill-wine does the same. They also prepare squill-vinegar: if someone takes of the squill-wine, before eating; if of the vinegar, after dinner. And marsh-wine — that is, the wine that comes to be in the marshes — is exceedingly healthy. And kiln-bread, formed thin and dried in the sun, is most useful toward health. If the water lying by should also be sickly, let it be boiled until a tenth of it is spent, then let it be cooled; and thus it will be harmless.
translator_notes: Cesti 2.6. οἶνος παρατραπείς is turned/soured wine. ἀψινθίτης / σκιλλίτης / ἕλειος οἶνος. κριβανίτης kiln-bread. Bracketed εἴην ὀσπρόν left unrestored. No Scripture.

title: A camp bolus so poison does not take you
english: Against being taken by a deleterious drug. So that we suffer nothing toward poison — there being two cures, of healing and of making it that one not suffer, and the second necessary — let someone, having become fasting of every putting-on, take twenty leaves of rue, two dried figs, and of walnuts an equal to the dried figs, and he would become unconquered to every drug; let a grain of salt also be present with these. Many bear witness by trial. Others, gathering more exactly, doubled the salt and the rue, and set twenty berries of pepper.

The more complete, which makes all drugs inactive and which is easy to carry in camp, is this: of fatty dried figs, and likewise of the brightest walnuts, and of dry rue, and also of ripe juniper berries, and still of Lemnian seal, equal parts, cut in a mortar and make little spheres the size of a Pontic nut, and take one each day.
translator_notes: Cesti 2.7. δηλητήριον is a deleterious drug. Restoration <τοῦ ἰᾶσθαι καὶ>. Λημνίας σφραγῖδος is Lemnian sealed earth. No Scripture.

title: Glue a great iron cut with the edible bulb
english: To glue a wound without a suture. Since in war some, being wounded, the division from iron being great, are the more subdued by sutures, toward this we found a natural help able to glue without a suture. It is this: pound the bulb which we eat, set it on, and it will glue beside.
translator_notes: Cesti 2.8. Restoration <τὸ>. βολβὸν ὃν ἐσθίομεν is the edible grape-hyacinth/bulb, not a generic 'bulb onion' forced. No Scripture.

title: Stop unstoppable blood with dried human blood
english: Toward blood flowing unstoppably. Take human blood, either from a vein-cutter or from any other manner it happens to come, and throw it into a wide-mouthed vessel.
